title: Domestic races differ like congeneric species, but usually less

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Domestic races differ like congeneric species, but usually less

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Apart from their lesser uniformity, their often monstrous development of one part, and their fertility when crossed, domestic races of a species differ from each other in the same manner as closely allied species of a genus in nature, though in most cases to a lesser degree.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: domestic races of the same species differ from each other in the same manner as, only in most cases in a lesser degree than, do closely-allied species of the same genus in a state of nature.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication”; section “Character of Domestic Varieties”. Scope: domestic races compared with closely allied wild congeneric species

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch01-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public morphology and sequence data support broad comparisons, but fertility, monstrosity and uniformity are not integrated. Conclusions will depend on trait and distance definitions.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Embed standardized morphology and fertility of domestic races and closely allied wild species in the same multivariate trait space. Compare effect sizes and directions of divergence; similar axes but usually smaller race distances support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Same manner' permits multiple metrics.

Cross-fertility data are sparse and nonstandard.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Genomic distances and scattered 3D scans can compare some breed pairs with some congeneric species, which is a proxy for 'same manner' and 'lesser degree'. No open dataset systematically measures the same characters in domestic races and wild congeners across animals and plants. The qualitative wording admits several morphometric operationalizations, so a single result would be only partly decisive.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Place domestic breeds and closely allied wild congeners in one morphospace and one genetic-distance matrix, then compare the axes that separate breeds with the axes that separate species and compare the magnitudes. Similar axes with smaller breed distances would support the statement; breed differences concentrated on different axes, or as large as species differences, would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Breed descriptors are categorical and uneven, while 3D coverage is sparse.

'Same manner' depends on which characters are measured and on how morphospaces are aligned.

Fertility when crossed and monstrous development, which the statement sets aside, are not in the same tables as shape.
